issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'I can talk about what happened very easily' conflicts with the other two memory items, which describe intrusive, sensory-dominated, repeatedly replaying trauma memories. That combination is not impossible, but with no other items indicating organized narrative access, the 'very easily' wording pulls in the opposite direction and is clinically inconsistent within this node.

issues.item: Memory: Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
issues.explanation: The trigger set is hard to reconcile with the trauma type of mugging/robbery. 'Being around children' and 'Happy families' do not show a plausible thematic link to the reported trauma, and there are no accompanying threat or appraisal items to explain why these social/family cues would specifically trigger this patient's robbery-related PTSD.

issues.item: Memory: Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.
issues.explanation: 'I pick arguments or create drama to distract myself from the trauma' is weakly supported by the rest of the profile. The formulation mainly links triggers and memory with maladaptive strategies, but the actual triggers and memory content given are socially/family themed and intrusive-image based; deliberate conflict-seeking does not fit clearly with those items and looks clinically disconnected from the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Triggers: Children Present: Being around children
issues.explanation: For a mugging/robbery trauma, triggers centered on children and idealized families are hard to link clinically unless there is additional trauma meaning not represented elsewhere. The memory items describe perceptual re-experiencing of the robbery, but these triggers imply family/child themes that are absent from the rest of the profile, making the trigger set feel disconnected from the trauma type.

Within the Triggers node, 'children present' and 'happy families' suggest a loss/family-comparison theme, whereas 'being criticised or corrected' suggests interpersonal shame or sensitivity. These could coexist, but together they do not form a coherent trigger pattern tied to a robbery, especially given no threat or appraisal items supporting these meanings.

'Happy families' is a weakly plausible trigger for a mugging/robbery trauma and is hard to connect to the accompanying memory items, which are purely sensory/reliving-based and suggest trauma reminders tied more directly to the event. It does not fit well with the otherwise robbery-linked trigger pattern.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Seeking Conflict: I pick arguments or create drama to distract myself from the trauma
issues.explanation: 'Seeking conflict/create drama' is not well supported by the rest of the profile. The formulation links triggers and memory to maladaptive strategies, but the selected triggers and memory items imply intrusive re-experiencing, for which suppression/avoidance is coherent; deliberate conflict-seeking appears clinically disconnected and unusually externalising relative to the rest of the profile.

vignette:
Kwame is a 58-year-old African American man who has worked as a hairdresser for many years, the kind of stylist who remembers clients' children's names and keeps a steady rhythm of conversation going while his hands work. He is married, and before the robbery he had been used to spending most of his day around people, moving easily between the intimacy of the salon chair and the bustle of the shop. The event he returns to in treatment happened after closing one evening, when he left the salon carrying the day's cash and supplies. A man approached him quickly, close enough that Kwame could smell alcohol on his breath before he fully understood what was happening. He remembers the encounter less as a story than as a series of sharp images: the man's face too near his own, the shine of a hand reaching into his jacket, the sudden angle of the sidewalk under the streetlight, the look of the bottle in the man's other hand, and the sense of being trapped in a moment that would not move forward. Even now, when he tries to describe it aloud, his speech stalls. He says he knows exactly what happened, but when he tries to put it into words, "it won't come out right," and he falls silent, seeing it instead.

In the weeks afterward, the robbery did not settle into the past for him. The memory came back as pictures and as a repeating sequence, like a film clip that started on its own. Sometimes it was the smell of alcohol that brought it on with particular force. If a client came in after lunch with liquor on his breath, or if he passed someone drinking from a paper bag on the walk to his car, Kwame would feel the whole scene return in images before he had even formed a thought about it. At other times it was less tangible but just as immediate: a person lingering too long near the front desk, someone watching the register, a stranger pacing outside the salon window. He found himself studying people closely for signs that they were not safe. He did not talk about this much, because he was trying very hard not to think about the robbery at all. He would interrupt the memory by forcing his attention elsewhere, cleaning his station repeatedly, turning on music, asking clients questions, anything to block the images once they started.

At the same time, he spent long stretches dwelling on what he believed he had done wrong. He replayed practical decisions-why he stayed late, why he carried the cash himself, why he did not notice the man sooner, whether he should have crossed the street or called his wife before leaving. The questions circled without relief. He had come to believe that he should have prevented it, that a man his age, with his experience of the city and of people, should have seen trouble coming. Being corrected by anyone began to strike that same raw place. If his wife reminded him he had forgotten groceries, or if a client told him he had trimmed a sideburn unevenly, the feeling that rose in him was disproportionate and immediate. Correction no longer felt like an ordinary part of work or marriage; it landed as proof, to him, that he was careless and had failed in ways he could not undo.

Over the following months, Kwame became quieter and more withdrawn. In a profession built around constant social contact, he started reducing the number of clients he would see, letting coworkers take walk-ins, avoiding casual conversation in the break room, and leaving the salon as soon as his last appointment was done. He preferred not to attend neighborhood gatherings or family events if there would be many people there, especially people he did not know. His wife noticed that he sat apart even at home, preoccupied and hard to reach. At the salon, the cost was practical as well as relational: regular clients commented that he seemed distracted, and one or two drifted to other stylists because he no longer had the warmth and ease they associated with him.

What finally brought Kwame to seek help was not a single new event but the recognition that his world had narrowed around the robbery. A recent afternoon in the salon made that plain. A client, mildly irritated, told him he needed the cut shorter around the ears, and at the same moment another man came in from outside carrying the smell of alcohol. Kwame froze for a second, images rushing up so vividly that he lost track of the conversation. Later he sat in his car, ashamed and shaken, thinking again of all the ways he had failed. By the time he came for treatment, he was exhausted by the effort of pushing the memory away and by how often it still returned. What frightened him most was the sense that he was no longer himself in the very place where he had always felt most competent. What he hoped for, cautiously, was to be able to work a full day, hear an ordinary correction, catch a stranger's scent of liquor, and remain in the present rather than being pulled back into those pictures.
